[[File:Gagea minima flower - Keila.jpg|thumb|''[[Gagea minima]]'' (least gagea)]]
'''''Gagea''''' is a large [[genus]] of [[Spring (season)|spring]] [[flower]]s in the [[Liliaceae|lily family]].<ref>Salisbury, Richard Anthony. 1806" ''Annals of Botany'' 2: 555</ref> ''Gagea'' species are perennially flowering plants.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schnittler |first1=Martin |last2=Nursafina |first2=Akmaral |last3=Peterson |first3=Angela |last4=Peterson |first4=Jens |last5=Barnick |first5=Carl |last6=Klahr |first6=Anja |date=3 October 2017 |title=Studies of life history of Gagea graeca (Liliaceae) based on morphological and molecular methods |journal=Botanical Studies |language=en |volume=58 |issue=1 |pages=40 |doi=10.1186/s40529-017-0194-6 |issn=1999-3110 |pmc=5626670 |pmid=28975526 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> It is found primarily in [[Eurasia]] with a few species extending into [[North Africa]] and one species (''[[Gagea serotina]]'') in [[North America]].<ref name="WCSP_280365"/><ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Zarrei |first1=M. |last2=Zarre |first2=S. |last3=Wilkin |first3=P. |last4=Rix |first4=M. |year=2007 |title=Systematic revision of the genus Gagea Salisb. (Liliaceae) in Iran |journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society |volume=154 |issue=4 |pages=559–588 |doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.2007.00678.x |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>Tison, J.M. (2009). An update of the genus ''Gagea'' Salisb. (Liliaceae) in the Iberian peninsula. Lagascalia 29: 7-22</ref><ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/flora.php?genere=Gagea Altervista Flora Italiana, genere ''Gagea'']</ref><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=113125 Flora of China Vol. 24 Page 117 <big>顶冰花属</big> ding bing hua shu ''Gagea'' Salisbury, Ann. Germ. Excurs. 102. 1830. ]</ref>

The genus is named after the [[England|English]] naturalist [[Thomas Gage (botanist)|Sir Thomas Gage]] (1781–1820). They were originally described as species of ''[[Ornithogalum]]'', which, together with the usual yellow colour of the flowers, explains the [[English language|English]] name '''yellow star-of-Bethlehem''' for the common European species, ''[[Gagea lutea]]''.<ref name="FE5">{{Cite book |title=Flora Europaea |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1980 |isbn=978-0-521-20108-7 |editor-last=Tutin |editor-first=T.G. |volume=5 |editor2-last=Heywood |editor2-first=V.H. |editor3-last=Burges |editor3-first=N.A. |editor4-last=Moore |editor4-first=D.M. |editor5-last=Valentine |editor5-first=D.H. |editor6-last=Walters |editor6-first=S.M. |editor7-last=Webb |editor7-first=D.A. |name-list-style=amp}} p. 25.</ref><ref name="WCSP_280365">{{Cite web |title=''Lloydia'' |url=http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=280365 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200726160147/https://wcsp.science.kew.org/namedetail.do?name_id=280365 |archive-date=26 July 2020 |access-date=9 January 2014 |work=[[World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]] |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]]}}</ref>

== Morphology ==
[[File:Gagea lutea sl3.jpg|thumb|''Gagea Lutea'' bulbous parts]]
The genus contains [[geophytes]] that use [[Bulb|bulbous]] parts to survive unfavorable conditions and quickly reproduce during favorable conditions. ''Gagea'' species have persistent [[Tepal|tepals]], and are generally smaller in size than other closely related genera in the Liliaceae family.<ref name="Zarrei 44–56">{{Cite journal |last1=Zarrei |first1=M. |last2=Wilkin |first2=P. |last3=Ingrouille |first3=M. J. |last4=Chase |first4=M. W. |date=28 January 2011 |title=A revised infrageneric classification for Gagea Salisb. (Tulipeae; Liliaceae): insights from DNA sequence and morphological data |url=https://phytotaxa.mapress.com/pt/article/view/phytotaxa.15.1.6 |journal=Phytotaxa |language=en |volume=15 |pages=44–56 |doi=10.11646/phytotaxa.15.1.6 |issn=1179-3163 |doi-access=free}}</ref> 

The genus has varied leaf morphology. However, it is common for them to have [[Leaf|basal leaves]], some of which are cauline. <ref name="Zarrei 44–56" />

Some species have [[Trichome|trichomes]]. These trichomes differ in their morphology. For instance, ''G. alberti'' and ''G. jensii'' have [[Trichome|dendroid-type trichomes]], but ''G. stepposa'' has [[Trichome|glandular trichomes]]. It is also common for ''Gagea'' species to have [[Stoma|amphistomatic stomata]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Qiu |first1=Juan |last2=Lin |first2=Musen |last3=Tan |first3=Dunyan |date=29 November 2023 |title=Taxonomic implications of leaf morphology and epidermal anatomy for 14 species of Gagea (Liliaceae) from Xinjiang, China |journal=Botanical Studies |language=en |volume=64 |issue=1 |pages=33 |doi=10.1186/s40529-023-00405-9 |issn=1999-3110 |pmc=10684841 |pmid=38017242 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Reproduction ==
''Gagea'' use two separate reproductive systems, [[Entomophily|insect pollination]] and [[Asexual reproduction|asexual]] [[bulbil]] reproduction.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Schnittler |first1=Martin |last2=Pfeiffer |first2=Tanja |last3=Harter |first3=David |last4=Hamann |first4=Anne |date=1 May 2009 |title=Bulbils contra seeds: reproductive investment in two species of Gagea (Liliaceae) |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00606-008-0143-7 |journal=Plant Systematics and Evolution |language=en |volume=279 |issue=1 |pages=29–40 |doi=10.1007/s00606-008-0143-7 |issn=1615-6110|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":2" /> There are two patterns of bulbil reproduction. In a more "continuous" mode, the plant "turns on" the ability to make bulbils, and continues to do so, only needing 2–10 millimeters cubed of total plant volume to begin [[vegetative reproduction]]. Once it reaches {{Convert abbreviated|100-300|mm3}} of volume, in some species, like ''[[Gagea lutea|G. lutea]]'', the plant stops bulbil reproduction to begin expending energy towards a flowering [[Phenology|phenophase]]. In some species, like ''[[Gagea spathacea|G. spathacea]]'', the plant never stops bulbil reproduction, and has no ability to reproduce [[Sexual reproduction|sexually]] (through flowering). <ref name=":1" />

It is common for ''Gagea'' species begin [[flowering]] early into spring.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Schnittler |first1=Martin |last2=Peterson |first2=Angela |last3=Peterson |first3=Jens |last4=Beisenova |first4=Saltanat |last5=Bersimbaev |first5=Rakhmetkazhi I. |last6=Pfeiffer |first6=Tanja |date=1 December 2013 |title=Minor differences with big consequences: Reproductive patterns in the genus Gagea (Liliaceae) |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0367253013000996 |journal=Flora - Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants |volume=208 |issue=10 |pages=591–598 |doi=10.1016/j.flora.2013.09.002 |issn=0367-2530 |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last1=Ninuola |first1=Sunmonu |last2=Kudo |first2=Gaku |date=October 2015 |title=Warm temperature conditions restrict the sexual reproduction and vegetative growth of the spring ephemeral Gagea lutea (Liliaceae) |url=https://eprints.lib.hokudai.ac.jp/repo/huscap/all/63014/ |access-date=2 February 2026 |website=Hokkaido University}}</ref> Many ''Gagea'' are [[Spring ephemeral|spring ephemerals]], and need to complete their flowering cycles before tree cover re-emerges. By mid-spring to summer, these species will store themselves in [[Bulb|bulbous]] parts underground in anticipation of the next flowering period.<ref name=":3" />

== Speciation/Adaptations ==
[[File:385 Gagea lutea, Gagea minima.jpg|thumb|''Gagea lutea'' fruit]]
During their flowering periods, species show different environmental [[Adaptation|adaptations]] based on their [[Habitat|habitats]]. ''G. ''sect. ''Platayspermum Boiss'' live in more [[Aridity|arid]] regions, where it is common for insects to feed upon any exposed [[Fruit|fruits]] or [[Seed|seeds]] from flowering plants. Therefore, the [[Taxonomy|sect]]. uses large, tough [[Sepal|sepals]] to ward off insects attempting to consume its fruit when it is in its developing phase.<ref name="Zarrei 44–56" /> Other [[Taxonomy|sects]], such as ''G. lutea'', commonly emerge immediately after snowmelt.<ref name=":3" /> Unlike in more arid regions, these species will have greener sepals after the flower is fully open.<ref name="Zarrei 44–56" />

[[Polyploidy]] and [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridization]], in the case of ''Gagea'', have large impacts on its ability to undergo [[speciation]], as evident in European species of the [[genus]].<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Pfeiffer |first1=Tanja |last2=Klahr |first2=Anja |last3=Peterson |first3=Angela |last4=Levichev |first4=Igor G. |last5=Schnittler |first5=Martin |date=May 2012 |title=No sex at all? Extremely low genetic diversity in Gagea spathacea (Liliaceae) across Europe |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0367253012000412 |journal=Flora - Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants |volume=207 |issue=5 |pages=372–378 |doi=10.1016/j.flora.2012.03.002 |issn=0367-2530|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Previous studies have shown that these two processes can significantly contribute to the process of speciation, while retaining [[fertility]] within a population.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Heimer |first1=Valentin |last2=Carnicero |first2=Pau |last3=Carrizo García |first3=Carolina |last4=Hilpold |first4=Andreas |last5=Dolenc Koce |first5=Jasna |last6=Leal |first6=J Luis |last7=Li |first7=Mingai |last8=Varotto |first8=Claudio |last9=Schönswetter |first9=Peter |last10=Frajman |first10=Božo |date=25 September 2025 |editor-last=Särkinen |editor-first=Tiina |title=Hybridization and Polyploidy Shaped the Evolutionary History of a Complex of Cryptic Species in European Woodrushes ( Luzula sect. Luzula ) |url=https://academic.oup.com/sysbio/advance-article/doi/10.1093/sysbio/syaf065/8263904 |journal=Systematic Biology |language=en |doi=10.1093/sysbio/syaf065 |issn=1063-5157 |pmid=40996468 |article-number=syaf065|hdl=10449/94775 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> ''Gagea'', therefore, has the ability to contain unique species such as ''[[Gagea spathacea|G. spathacea]]'', being a [[Polyploidy|nonaploid]] that causes the plant to be limited in [[Post-zygotic isolation|post-zygotic]] reproduction. The species has spread across [[Central Europe]], the [[Caucasus]], [[Sweden]], [[Denmark]], the [[Netherlands]], and [[Belgium]] with little to no [[Genetics|genetic]] differences due to its use of [[Clonal reproduction|clonal]] reproduction. However, through polyploidy and hybridization events, it still retains the ability to undergo [[evolution]]. <ref name=":4" />
